question: A 7-year-old boy has daytime asthma symptoms 3–4 times per week, one night-time awakening per week due to wheeze, and his spirometry shows FEV1 72% predicted with ≥12% reversibility after salbutamol. He has never received a controller medication. According to GINA guidelines, which of the following best describes his asthma severity and the appropriate initial controller therapy?

answers.text: Mild intermittent asthma; no controller needed, salbutamol reliever only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intermittent asthma is characterised by symptoms ≤2 days per week, no night-time symptoms, and FEV1 ≥80% predicted. This child has daytime symptoms 3–4 times per week and nocturnal awakening — he exceeds the intermittent threshold and requires a controller.

answers.text: Mild persistent asthma; low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as controller

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mild persistent asthma: symptoms >2 days/week but not daily, 3–4 night awakenings/month (1/week fits here), FEV1 ≥80% — though his FEV1 of 72% places him at the boundary, the frequency pattern aligns with mild persistent. GINA Step 2 recommends low-dose ICS (e.g. budesonide 200 mcg/day or beclomethasone equivalent) as the preferred controller, with SABA reliever.

answers.text: Moderate persistent asthma; low-dose ICS plus long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) as controller

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Moderate persistent asthma features daily symptoms, weekly night awakenings, and FEV1 60–80%. While his FEV1 is borderline, his symptom frequency (not daily) is below the moderate persistent threshold. LABA is never used as monotherapy in children and should not be added until low-dose ICS alone has been trialled at GINA Step 2.

answers.text: Severe persistent asthma; high-dose ICS plus oral corticosteroids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Severe persistent asthma means continual daytime symptoms, frequent night awakenings, FEV1 <60%, and significantly limited activity. This child does not meet these criteria. Jumping to high-dose ICS and oral corticosteroids without a trial of lower-step therapy is incorrect and exposes the child to unnecessary side effects.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the GINA severity classification grid: intermittent (≤2 days/week, no night symptoms, FEV1 ≥80%), mild persistent (>2 days/week but not daily, 3–4 night awakenings/month, FEV1 ≥80%), moderate persistent (daily symptoms, weekly night awakenings, FEV1 60–80%), severe persistent (continual symptoms, frequent night awakenings, FEV1 <60%). Match symptom pattern to step, then choose the controller.

Well done. Classifying severity correctly (using symptom frequency, nocturnal symptoms, and spirometry) drives the step of therapy. Low-dose ICS monotherapy is the cornerstone for mild persistent asthma in children — safe, effective, and the GINA-recommended first-line controller.
